case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Colorado may, consistent with the First Amendment, discipline a licensed counselor for engaging in certain talk-therapy communications with a minor client—i.e., whether the State may treat the counselor’s speech in therapy as regulable professional “conduct” (or as content-based speech subject to heightened scrutiny).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (Free Speech Clause) (and, as applied, Colorado’s licensed-mental-health regulation restricting certain counseling practices with minors commonly characterized as a ban on “conversion therapy” or sexual-orientation/gender-identity change efforts).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner contends that the Colorado regime is a content- and viewpoint-based restriction on speech because it turns on what the counselor says in a private therapeutic setting (permitting affirming counseling while prohibiting counseling that explores or supports movement away from certain identities or behaviors). Petitioner argues that calling the restriction “professional conduct” cannot avoid First Amendment scrutiny where the regulated activity is communication itself, and that the law fails heightened scrutiny because it suppresses one side of a contested debate, chills core expressive activity (counseling), and is not narrowly tailored to prevent harm.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents contend the law is a permissible regulation of professional practice aimed at protecting minors’ health and safety, and that it targets harmful treatment methods rather than ideas. On this view, the State may set standards of care for licensed providers, and any burden on speech is incidental to regulating professional conduct within the counselor-client relationship; therefore the law should receive deferential review (or at most intermediate scrutiny) and be upheld because it serves compelling/important interests in preventing harm to minors and maintaining professional ethics.
key_precedents: National Institute of Family & Life Advocates v. Becerra (NIFLA) (2018)
King v. Governor of New Jersey (3d Cir. 2014)
Otto v. City of Boca Raton (11th Cir. 2020)
Rumsfeld v. Forum for Academic & Institutional Rights, Inc. (FAIR) (2006)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch make the Petitioners’ strongest point: the statute’s trigger tracks the content (and arguably the viewpoint) of what is said in the counseling room, so Reed/NIFLA caution against letting the State repackage speech regulation as “standards of care.” But NIFLA also expressly preserves regulation of professional conduct that incidentally involves speech, and I agree with Justice Kagan that we can decide this on narrow, as-applied grounds limited to licensed clinicians providing treatment to minors within a fiduciary relationship—without creating a broad “professional speech” exception. Casey is not a perfect fit, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, yet it supports the more general proposition that regulation of medical practice can include speech components without automatically triggering the full Reed framework as if we were policing public debate. Under a minimalist approach, the better course is to uphold this as a standard-of-care rule for minor patients while leaving open future challenges where the State’s line-drawing more clearly operates as viewpoint suppression outside the treatment relationship.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s effort to cabin this as regulation of “professional conduct that incidentally involves speech” fails because the statute defines the prohibited “treatment” by the communicative content and direction of the counselor’s words in a talk-therapy session; that is regulation of speech as speech, not conduct with incidental speech. NIFLA rejects a free-floating “professional speech” carveout, and the conduct/incidental-speech passage cannot be used—as Justice Kavanaugh notes—to let States relabel viewpoint-based restrictions as “standard of care” simply because the speaker is licensed. Justice Alito’s reliance on Casey underscores the distinction: informed-consent rules attach to a procedure and require disclosure; here the State bans one side of a private conversational exchange, which triggers heightened scrutiny under Reed’s content-based framework and is irreconcilable with the First Amendment’s original public meaning. The State’s interest in protecting minors is weighty, but it cannot justify categorical suppression of disfavored viewpoints in private counseling absent narrow tailoring that this law, by its terms, lacks.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas are right that the statute’s trigger is the content of what is said in the counseling room, which squarely raises Reed/NIFLA concerns and cannot be waved away by labels. But NIFLA also expressly preserves state authority to regulate professional conduct that incidentally involves speech, and I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that—properly cabined—this operates as a licensure-enforceable standard-of-care rule governing a defined treatment modality for minors within a fiduciary clinical relationship, not a censorship regime for public discourse. Reed’s sign-code logic should not be transplanted mechanically into malpractice/discipline settings without destabilizing routine regulation of medical and mental-health practice and effectively constitutionalizing contested treatment judgments. Petitioners’ viewpoint-discrimination framing remains overbroad because the law does not silence counselors as speakers in the general marketplace of ideas; it restricts what licensed professionals may provide as treatment to minors, where States have long had latitude to draw cautious lines to protect patients.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett make the strongest point that the statute’s trigger tracks communicative content in talk therapy, which raises a serious Reed/NIFLA concern and the risk of States relabeling viewpoint discrimination as “standards of care.” But NIFLA itself preserves a lane for regulation of professional conduct that incidentally involves speech, and—on Chief Justice Roberts’s narrower framing—this law is best treated as an as-applied licensure/standard-of-care rule governing a defined treatment modality for minors within a fiduciary clinical relationship, not as censorship of ideas in public discourse. Reed’s sign-code logic should not be imported mechanically into the State’s traditional oversight of medical practice where speech is the instrument of treatment, or we will constitutionalize contested mental-health standards and disable ordinary protections for vulnerable minors. The fact that clinicians remain free to express identical viewpoints outside the clinical modality, and to provide other counseling within the session, confirms for me this is regulation of treatment practice rather than a broad ideological orthodoxy.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas press the strongest point: this statute’s trigger is what is said in the counseling room, which looks facially content-based under Reed and thus suspicious under NIFLA’s warning against a “professional speech” carveout. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that NIFLA itself preserves a distinct lane for regulating professional conduct that incidentally involves speech, and the better textual/pragmatic fit here is a licensure-enforceable definition of a prohibited treatment modality for minors within a fiduciary clinical relationship, not a general suppression of ideas. Reed’s sign-code framework is a poor proxy for how States historically set enforceable standards of care, and treating every speech-mediated treatment rule as strict-scrutiny speech censorship would constitutionalize routine professional discipline in a way NIFLA did not require. The narrow holding Roberts sketches—limited to licensed treatment of minors and leaving open broader viewpoint-discrimination questions outside the clinical context—addresses Petitioners’ end-run concern without resurrecting “professional speech” as a freestanding category.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow, as-applied framing—treating this as a standard-of-care rule regulating “professional conduct that incidentally involves speech”—is the strongest counter, and I take seriously the State’s traditional authority over licensure and minors. But as Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett emphasize, the statute defines the forbidden “treatment” by the communicative content and direction of the therapist’s words, allowing “affirming” messages while banning counseling aimed at change; that is facially content-based (and plausibly viewpoint-based) under Reed, not an incidental speech burden attached to nonexpressive conduct. NIFLA’s preserved lane for incidental-speech regulation cannot be expanded into a relabeling device that converts direct speech restrictions into “conduct” whenever the speaker is licensed, or else we recreate the very “professional speech” carveout NIFLA rejected. Even crediting Justice Sotomayor’s harm concerns, strict scrutiny can accommodate compelling interests, and on this record a categorical message-based ban is difficult to square with narrow tailoring.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s narrow, as-applied approach—treating this as a licensure “standard of care” within a fiduciary relationship—has real institutional appeal and is the strongest argument for the Respondent, especially given NIFLA’s acknowledgement that States may regulate professional conduct that incidentally involves speech. But here the statute does not merely incidentally burden speech in the course of regulating nonexpressive conduct; as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, it defines the prohibited “treatment” by the communicative content and direction of what is said in talk therapy, which is precisely what triggers Reed/NIFLA heightened scrutiny concerns. Casey’s informed-consent paradigm (invoked by Roberts and Kagan) is materially different because it compels disclosures ancillary to a procedure rather than categorically forbidding one set of therapeutic messages while permitting the opposite within the same professional setting. Accepting the State’s relabeling on this record risks creating an end-run around NIFLA by allowing viewpoint- or content-based bans to be recast as “substandard care” without the narrow tailoring that strict scrutiny demands, even crediting Justice Sotomayor’s point about the weighty interest in protecting minors.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s narrow framing—treating this as a licensure “standard of care” regulating professional conduct that incidentally involves speech—does not fit the statute’s operative mechanics on this record, because the prohibited “treatment” is defined by the communicative content and direction of the counselor’s words in talk therapy. NIFLA’s preserved lane for incidental-speech regulation (and Casey’s informed-consent analogy) concerns disclosures or speech tethered to nonexpressive conduct or procedures; here, as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, the conduct is the speech itself, so Reed’s content-based analysis is properly triggered and cannot be avoided by relabeling. I take seriously Justice Sotomayor’s concern that strict scrutiny could constitutionalize clinical disputes, but NIFLA itself rejected a free-floating “professional speech” carveout, and permitting content-defined bans in the clinical setting would recreate that exception under another name. Even crediting the State’s compelling interest in protecting minors, the categorical, message-based prohibition is unlikely to be narrowly tailored, and precedent as invoked by Roberts and Kagan does not genuinely undermine the First Amendment problem I see.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the hardest point: the statute’s trigger is the communicative content of what happens in-session, so Reed/NIFLA push toward heightened scrutiny. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that NIFLA’s preserved lane for regulating professional conduct that incidentally involves speech can apply where the State is defining an enforceable standard of care for licensed treatment of minors within a fiduciary relationship, rather than suppressing ideas in public debate. Reed’s sign-code logic does not translate cleanly to licensure discipline, and Casey—while not a perfect match—supports the broader proposition that States may regulate medical practice even when speech is the means, especially to protect minors. Under a pragmatic, narrow as-applied approach, the law’s practical effect is to discipline a disputed treatment modality for minors while leaving ample room for clinicians to express or advocate the underlying views outside the therapeutic intervention, which keeps this from becoming a general viewpoint-censorship regime.

John Roberts.reasoning: Colorado’s rule can be sustained as a regulation of licensed professional conduct—setting a standard of care for treatment of minors—even though the treatment is delivered through words, because this Court has recognized that States may regulate “professional conduct that incidentally involves speech.” NIFLA rejected a freestanding “professional speech” category, but it reaffirmed that licensing regimes may constitutionally prescribe or proscribe communications when they are part of the practice of medicine or counseling and tied to a legally defined standard of care, rather than a general public debate. A narrow disposition upholding the statute as applied to licensed counselors treating minors preserves federalism and institutional legitimacy while avoiding a broad ruling about all therapist-client speech under the First Amendment. On that understanding, heightened scrutiny is not automatically triggered merely because talk-therapy is speech, and the State’s interest in protecting minors’ health and safety supports the regulation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction targets what a counselor may say to a minor in a private therapeutic setting and thus operates as a content- and viewpoint-based regulation of speech under the First Amendment, not merely a regulation of conduct. This Court in NIFLA v. Becerra rejected a lower-scrutiny category of “professional speech,” making clear that content-based burdens on speech do not become exempt from heightened scrutiny simply because they occur within a licensed professional relationship. Under Reed v. Town of Gilbert, a law that turns on the communicative content of the message triggers strict scrutiny, and the State cannot evade that by relabeling speech as “treatment.” Because the statute suppresses one side of a contested moral and scientific debate and compels an orthodoxy in counseling, it is inconsistent with the First Amendment’s original public meaning and must be struck down as applied to talk therapy.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction operates as a regulation of licensed professional practice directed at a state-defined standard of care for minors, and the First Amendment does not disable the State from disciplining practitioners for providing treatment the State reasonably deems harmful. NIFLA v. Becerra rejected a freestanding, lesser-protected category of “professional speech,” but it reaffirmed that States may regulate “professional conduct” that incidentally involves speech, citing Casey’s informed-consent framework; talk-therapy delivered as treatment within a licensed relationship can fit that model. Unlike the sign code in Reed v. Town of Gilbert, this law is better understood as governing what a licensed counselor may do to a minor patient as treatment, not as suppressing public debate, and the practical consequence of invalidation would be to constitutionalize disputed standards of mental-health care and curtail States’ traditional police-power oversight of licensure. Given the State’s substantial interest in protecting minors and maintaining professional standards, and the limited context of regulated treatment delivered under color of a state license, heightened scrutiny is not warranted and the regulation should be sustained.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction operates as a regulation of licensed professional practice to protect minors from documented harms, and any burden on speech is incidental to enforcing a standard of care within the counselor–client relationship. NIFLA rejected a freestanding “professional speech” category, but it reaffirmed that a State may regulate “professional conduct” that “incidentally involves speech,” including standards governing what licensed professionals may say in providing treatment. Unlike the ordinance in Reed v. Town of Gilbert, this law is best understood as a health-and-safety measure defining unethical or harmful treatment methods for minors, not as a general suppression of ideas in public discourse. Given the State’s compelling interest in safeguarding vulnerable minors and maintaining professional ethics, the discipline is consistent with the First Amendment as applied to licensed counseling practice.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction operates as a regulation of licensed professional practice directed at a particular treatment modality for minors, and any burden on speech is incidental to defining the standard of care within a therapist–client relationship. NIFLA rejects a free-floating “professional speech” category but expressly preserves the State’s authority to regulate professional conduct that “incidentally involves speech,” citing Casey’s informed-consent framework; this law fits more naturally on that side of the line than on Reed’s paradigm of public-facing content discrimination. The statute is also materially unlike compelled-speech regimes because it does not force the counselor to affirm any message; it prohibits a defined practice with a vulnerable population, a sphere where States traditionally receive latitude to protect health and safety. Given the State’s substantial interest in safeguarding minors and maintaining professional ethics, the regulation is workable and coherent as a licensing standard rather than a viewpoint-based censorship scheme.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Colorado’s law turns on the content (and effectively the viewpoint) of what a counselor says in a therapy session—permitting “affirming” counseling while prohibiting counseling that explores change—and so triggers heightened scrutiny under the Free Speech Clause, not a deferential “professional conduct” test. In NIFLA v. Becerra, this Court rejected a freestanding “professional speech” category subject to lesser protection and cautioned that content-based regulation of speech remains presumptively unconstitutional even when it occurs in a professional setting. While a State may regulate professional conduct that only incidentally involves speech (as in Casey’s informed-consent context), a prohibition aimed at specific therapeutic messages is not merely incidental; it is regulation of speech itself. Under Reed v. Town of Gilbert’s content-based framework, the State must satisfy strict scrutiny, and a categorical ban on disfavored counseling viewpoints is unlikely to be narrowly tailored to preventing harm to minors.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction singles out particular therapeutic communications based on their content and, as alleged, their viewpoint—permitting counseling that affirms certain identities while prohibiting counseling that explores change—triggering heightened First Amendment scrutiny under Reed v. Town of Gilbert. NIFLA rejects a freewheeling “professional speech” exception and makes clear that States may not evade First Amendment review by re-labeling speech as professional “conduct” when the regulated activity is the communication itself, as in talk therapy. While States have latitude to regulate professional conduct that incidentally burdens speech, this law’s operative line is drawn by what the counselor says, not by nonexpressive conduct, and thus cannot be sustained on mere deference to licensing authority. Given that the law targets one side of a contested debate within a private counseling relationship, it is presumptively invalid and must satisfy strict scrutiny, which the State has not shown on this record.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction turns on the content of what a licensed counselor says in a talk-therapy session with a minor—permitting counseling that affirms certain identities or outcomes while prohibiting counseling that explores or supports movement away from them—so it is a content-based (and plausibly viewpoint-based) regulation of speech presumptively subject to strict scrutiny under the First Amendment. NIFLA rejected a freestanding “professional speech” category with diminished protection, making it insufficient for the State to relabel speech as professional “conduct” where the regulated activity is communication itself. While States may regulate professional conduct and impose licensing standards, see NIFLA, that authority does not allow them to single out disfavored messages within private counseling conversations without meeting heightened scrutiny. On this record, the law’s speech-based line-drawing is difficult to reconcile with Reed’s demand for narrow tailoring when the government regulates speech based on its communicative content.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction is best understood as a regulation of the licensed practice of mental-health treatment for minors—i.e., a standard-of-care rule governing what therapeutic interventions a professional may administer to a vulnerable client—rather than a general public suppression of ideas, and States have substantial latitude to set such licensing conditions to protect health and safety. Under NIFLA, there is no free-floating “professional speech” category, but the Court reaffirmed that government may regulate professional conduct that incidentally involves speech; here, the State is regulating a therapeutic modality within a fiduciary, clinician–patient relationship with minors, not compelling counselors to espouse the State’s views in public discourse. Reed’s content-based framework does not mechanically apply in the same way where the law targets the provision of a licensed treatment to minors and leaves ample alternative channels for counselors to express their views outside the treatment context. Given the practical consequences for minors and the State’s interest in preventing harm, I would uphold the law as a permissible health-and-safety regulation of professional practice consistent with the First Amendment.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Colorado may, consistent with the First Amendment, discipline a licensed mental-health professional for engaging in certain counseling conversations with a client—i.e., restrict what the counselor may say in therapy—by characterizing the restriction as regulation of “professional conduct.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (Free Speech Clause), as applied to Colorado’s regulation of licensed mental-health professionals that prohibits specified counseling practices/conversations (commonly referred to as a ban on “conversion therapy” for minors).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner contends Colorado’s law is a content-based (and viewpoint-discriminatory) restriction on speech because it singles out particular messages and therapeutic viewpoints expressed in talk therapy, triggering strict scrutiny. She argues the State cannot evade First Amendment review by relabeling speech as “professional conduct,” especially where the regulated activity is communication itself. Petitioner and supporting amici emphasize that counseling is fundamentally speech, that clients should be able to seek voluntary counseling consistent with their values (including religious convictions), and that the law impermissibly censors one side of a contested public and scientific debate.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents maintain the law regulates professional conduct within a licensed healthcare relationship to protect minors from harmful practices, and any burden on speech is incidental to valid regulation of treatment. They argue the State has longstanding authority to set standards of care for licensed professionals, that the restriction targets a specific practice deemed harmful (not ideas as such), and that heightened First Amendment scrutiny is not appropriate because the law functions like other professional regulations (e.g., prohibitions on fraudulent, dangerous, or substandard treatment). Respondent-aligned amici (including former conversion-therapy leaders) stress asserted harms and the State’s protective and medical-consensus-based rationale.
key_precedents: National Institute of Family and Life Advocates v. Becerra (NIFLA) (2018)
Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania v. Casey (1992)
West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette (1943)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point—that States may set ex ante standards of care for minors within a licensed fiduciary relationship, and that NIFLA preserves regulation of professional conduct even when carried out through words—has force, and we should say so. But as Justice Kavanaugh stresses, this statute does not regulate a generally applicable malpractice duty or a Casey-type disclosure; it defines the forbidden “practice” by the content and intended direction of the counseling conversation itself, which squarely triggers Reed/NIFLA concerns about relabeling censorship as professional regulation. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project does not carry the needed weight here because Holder’s coordinated-services and national-security context does not establish a general rule permitting viewpoint-laden bans on private, consensual therapeutic dialogue. To protect institutional legitimacy, I would maintain a narrow, as-applied holding: on this record Colorado has not shown sufficiently tailored justification for a content-based restriction on noncoercive talk therapy with a willing minor, while preserving robust state authority to police coercion, fraud, and negligence through viewpoint-neutral standards.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that Colorado is merely regulating a treatment modality within a fiduciary, licensed relationship for minors—still fails on a textualist account because the statute defines the forbidden “practice” by the content and communicative aim of the counseling itself, making it a content-based (and often viewpoint-based) speech restriction under Reed and NIFLA, not a regulation of nonexpressive conduct with incidental speech effects. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project does not alter that conclusion: Holder addressed coordinated services to designated foreign terrorist organizations in a distinct national-security setting, and it cannot be generalized to permit the State to suppress one side of a disputed conversation between counselor and client simply because it occurs in a professional office. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow, as-applied disposition reinforces the methodological point that the State’s licensing power cannot be used as an end-run around the First Amendment where the trigger for liability is what the speaker says and intends to communicate. Because Colorado retains viewpoint-neutral tools (fraud, coercion, negligence/malpractice, and disclosure rules) to protect minors, this categorical ban is not narrowly tailored under heightened scrutiny.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that States may set standards of care for minors in a licensed fiduciary relationship and that NIFLA preserves regulation of professional conduct even when carried out through words. But this statute does not regulate a generally applicable duty of care or a Casey-style disclosure; it defines the prohibited “practice” by the communicative content and therapeutic aim of the counseling itself, which is exactly the sort of relabeling of censorship as “conduct” NIFLA warns against. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Holder does not move me because Holder involved coordinated services to foreign terrorist organizations and a distinct national-security framework; it cannot justify viewpoint-tilted bans on private, consensual therapeutic dialogue. Given available, less speech-restrictive alternatives (fraud, coercion, negligence standards), Colorado has not shown narrow tailoring under strict scrutiny, so I remain with the petitioner.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point seriously: the statute’s trigger is what is said and the counselor’s intended therapeutic aim, which makes Reed/NIFLA content-discrimination concerns real. But NIFLA’s own carve-out matters here: it preserves state authority to regulate professional conduct and standards of care where speech is the vehicle for delivering treatment, and this law operates only within a state-created, fiduciary licensing relationship with minors—far from the public marketplace that Reed presupposes. Justice Thomas’s framing of this as “prohibiting one side of a contested discussion” overreads the statute’s function; it does not ban advocacy or compel orthodoxy, it restricts a particular treatment modality the State has reasonably found harmful for minors, while leaving room for supportive, exploratory counseling. I am not persuaded that the Constitution forces States to proceed only case-by-case through negligence actions (as the Chief suggests) when they have long been able to proscribe harmful medical practices for minors ex ante, even if the practice is administered through words; I would uphold on this record while leaving room for as-applied challenges if enforcement devolves into viewpoint policing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh press the hardest point: the statute keys liability to the content and therapeutic aim of what the counselor says, which looks like a Reed/NIFLA content-based restriction rather than Casey-style informed-consent. But I think that framing still abstracts away the legally salient setting—a state-licensed, fiduciary treatment relationship with minors—where the State has longstanding authority to define standards of care, and NIFLA (while rejecting a freestanding “professional speech” category) preserves regulation of professional conduct even when speech is the vehicle for delivering the service. Justice Thomas’s orthodoxy analogy and the petitioners’ reliance on “less restrictive” malpractice after-the-fact strikes me as incomplete: States often draw ex ante lines against practices they reasonably deem harmful to minors, and the question is whether this is a genuine modality-of-treatment line rather than viewpoint policing. That said, Roberts’s suggested narrowness highlights a real tailoring/administrability risk, so my confidence remains modest and I would scrutinize applications that drift into suppressing exploration or supportive counseling rather than prohibiting the targeted practice.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the best point: States may set standards of care for minors and, per NIFLA, sometimes regulate professional conduct even when it is carried out through words. But this statute defines the regulated “conduct” by the content and communicative aim of the counseling conversation itself, which places it in Reed/NIFLA territory rather than Casey’s limited informed-consent framework (factual, noncontroversial disclosures) or a viewpoint-neutral malpractice regime. Justice Kagan’s invocation of Holder does not move me because Holder involved coordinated services to designated foreign terrorist organizations in a national-security setting, not a categorical, message-directed ban on private, consensual therapeutic dialogue; extending it here would effectively recreate the “professional speech” carveout NIFLA rejected. As Chief Justice Roberts suggests, the State retains ample room to police coercion, fraud, and negligence through neutral rules, so Colorado has not shown narrow tailoring under the requisite heightened scrutiny on this record.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan make the best point that States retain broad authority to define standards of care for minors within a licensed, fiduciary relationship, and NIFLA preserves regulation of professional conduct even when carried out through words. But as the Chief Justice underscores, this statute does not function like Casey’s informed-consent regime or a neutral malpractice rule; it defines the prohibited “practice” by the content and therapeutic aim of the counseling conversation itself, which under Reed and NIFLA triggers heightened scrutiny rather than deference. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Holder does not move me because its coordinated-support/national-security context is a poor fit for viewpoint-tilted censorship of private, consensual talk therapy, and adopting it here would effectively resurrect the “professional speech” carveout NIFLA rejected. Keeping the holding narrow for institutional reasons, I would rule for petitioners as applied to noncoercive conversational therapy while leaving room for viewpoint-neutral regulation of coercion, fraud, and negligence.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point—that Colorado is setting a standard of care for minors within a licensed fiduciary relationship and thus regulating conduct with only incidental speech effects—does not fit this statute’s text as applied to talk therapy, because the law defines the prohibited “practice” by the content and intended communicative aim of the counseling conversation itself. Under NIFLA, the State may regulate professional conduct, but it cannot evade heightened scrutiny by relabeling a content-based speech restriction as “conduct,” and Reed’s framework is triggered where liability turns on what is said and toward what end. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project does not undermine that conclusion because Holder rested on coordinated support to foreign terrorist organizations in a distinct national-security setting, not private, consensual therapeutic dialogue; importing Holder here would effectively recreate the freestanding “professional speech” carveout NIFLA rejected. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts’s as-applied narrowing: on this record Colorado has not shown the categorical, message-defined prohibition is narrowly tailored, while leaving room for viewpoint-neutral malpractice, coercion, and fraud regulation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s point—that the statute’s trigger tracks conversational content and therapeutic aim, raising Reed/NIFLA red flags—is the petitioners’ best argument, and I agree it creates real First Amendment pressure on the State. But NIFLA also preserves a State’s authority to regulate professional conduct within a licensing regime, and here the regulation operates only inside a fiduciary therapist–minor relationship as a prophylactic standard-of-care judgment about a treatment modality, not as a ban on public advocacy or a compelled-orthodoxy rule of the Barnette/Wooley sort that Justice Thomas emphasizes. Pragmatically, treating every talk-therapy standard as presumptively subject to strict scrutiny would constitutionalize medical disputes and destabilize ordinary health-and-safety regulation for minors; I would uphold on this record while leaving room for as-applied challenges if enforcement morphs into viewpoint-policing rather than genuine professional-care regulation. Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project, though different (as Roberts notes), still supports the narrower proposition that speech can be regulable as part of delivering a regulated service, reinforcing my view that the professional-context frame matters here.

John Roberts.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction targets what a licensed counselor may say in talk therapy based on the content and viewpoint of the message, triggering serious First Amendment concerns under Reed v. Town of Gilbert and this Court’s compelled/forbidden-speech cases. NIFLA rejected a freestanding “professional speech” doctrine and cautioned that States may not evade heightened scrutiny by relabeling speech regulations as professional regulation; while States may regulate professional conduct that incidentally involves speech (as in Casey’s informed-consent context), this law regulates the counseling conversation itself rather than requiring disclosure of factual, noncontroversial information. Given the need for narrow grounds and institutional legitimacy, I would hold only that, as applied to purely conversational therapy, Colorado has not shown a sufficiently tailored justification to sustain a content-based restriction on speech. The State remains free to regulate malpractice, coercion, and nonconsensual or physically dangerous conduct through generally applicable standards of care.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Colorado’s statute targets what a therapist may say to a client by prohibiting counseling that seeks particular outcomes with respect to sexual orientation or gender identity, making it a content-based—and in operation viewpoint-based—restriction on speech under Reed v. Town of Gilbert. NIFLA rejected a free-floating “professional speech” doctrine and permits regulation of professional conduct that only incidentally involves speech, but here the regulated “conduct” is the counseling conversation itself rather than a nonexpressive medical procedure, so the First Amendment is directly implicated. Like Barnette and Wooley, the State may not prescribe orthodoxy in matters of opinion by censoring one side of a contested moral and scientific debate, even within a licensed relationship, absent satisfaction of strict scrutiny. A State’s power to license and set standards of care does not include authority to suppress disfavored viewpoints in private speech between counselor and willing client.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Colorado’s law, as applied to talk therapy, regulates speech itself: it restricts what a licensed counselor may say to a client based on the content and viewpoint of the message (permitting counseling that affirms certain sexual-orientation or gender-identity outcomes while prohibiting counseling aimed at other outcomes), which triggers heightened scrutiny under Reed v. Town of Gilbert. NIFLA rejected a free-floating “professional speech” category that would allow States to dilute First Amendment protection simply because speech occurs within a licensed professional-client relationship; relabeling speech as “professional conduct” cannot evade that rule where the regulated ‘conduct’ is communication. While the State has strong interests in protecting minors and regulating medical practice, this statute is not a generally applicable standard-of-care rule but a targeted ban on disfavored counseling conversations, and the practical consequence of upholding it would be broad governmental power to censor contested viewpoints in therapeutic settings. Accordingly, the First Amendment forbids disciplining the petitioner for engaging in voluntary counseling conversations with her clients on this basis.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction operates as regulation of professional conduct within a licensed therapeutic relationship—setting a standard of care for treatment of minors—rather than a general suppression of ideas, and the First Amendment permits such regulation even when the conduct is carried out through words. Under NIFLA, the Court declined to create a broad “professional speech” exemption, but reaffirmed that States may regulate speech “as part of the practice of” a profession when doing so enforces professional standards and only incidentally burdens speech. As in Casey, where informed-consent requirements were upheld as part of medical practice, Colorado may define and prohibit a treatment it reasonably deems harmful to protect vulnerable patients (minors) without triggering strict scrutiny applicable to public forum speech regulations like Reed. Given the State’s compelling protective interest in minors and its traditional authority over licensing and standards of care, the law is best understood as a permissible professional regulation under the First Amendment.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: NIFLA makes clear there is no freestanding “professional speech” category exempt from First Amendment scrutiny, but it also recognizes that States may regulate professional conduct and that any speech burden can be incidental when the law targets treatment within the professional-client relationship. Colorado’s law operates as a standard-of-care rule for licensed mental-health practice directed at a specific therapeutic practice with minors, not a general public ban on expressing ideas, and the State’s longstanding licensing authority supports a more deferential approach than strict scrutiny in this setting. Under Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project, the fact that a regulated course of professional service is carried out through words does not automatically convert it into constitutionally protected advocacy immune from regulation. Given the State’s compelling interest in protecting minors and the workability of allowing health-and-safety standards for licensed treatment, I would uphold the law as regulating professional conduct with, at most, incidental effects on speech consistent with the First Amendment.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Colorado’s law restricts what a licensed counselor may say in a counseling session based on the content and viewpoint of the message (permitting some therapeutic conversations about sexual orientation/gender identity while forbidding others), which triggers strict scrutiny under the First Amendment. This Court in NIFLA rejected a freestanding “professional speech” category and held that content-based regulations of speech do not escape ordinary First Amendment review merely because they occur in a professional-client relationship. Labeling the restriction “professional conduct” cannot change the analysis where the regulated “conduct” is the communication itself, and Reed confirms that facially content-based rules demand the most exacting review. On this record, the State may regulate licensing and malpractice, but it cannot censor disfavored viewpoints in talk therapy consistent with the Free Speech Clause (U.S. Const. amend. I).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Colorado’s law, as applied to talk therapy, regulates the content and viewpoint of what a licensed counselor may say to a client, triggering strict scrutiny under the First Amendment rather than being insulated as mere regulation of “professional conduct.” NIFLA rejected a freestanding “professional speech” category and allowed diminished scrutiny only for (i) compelled disclosure of factual, noncontroversial information and (ii) regulation of conduct that only incidentally burdens speech—neither of which fits a ban aimed at particular counseling messages. Under Reed, a restriction that turns on the topic and viewpoint of the communication is presumptively unconstitutional, and the State cannot evade that by relabeling speech as treatment. Given the Court’s traditional reluctance to create new carveouts from core speech protection and the workability concerns of allowing states to censor disfavored therapeutic viewpoints, the First Amendment requires heightened scrutiny here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Colorado’s law, as applied to talk therapy, regulates speech because the prohibited “practice” consists of particular counseling conversations and messages, making it content-based (and plausibly viewpoint-based) under Reed v. Town of Gilbert. NIFLA rejects a free-floating “professional speech” category warranting diminished First Amendment protection, and permits treating speech as conduct only in narrow contexts like informed-consent disclosures or traditional malpractice regulation—neither of which fits a categorical ban on specified viewpoints in counseling. While States have substantial authority to regulate professional conduct and protect minors, they cannot evade heightened First Amendment scrutiny by relabeling communicative treatment as “conduct,” especially where discipline turns on what the counselor may say. Accordingly, Colorado must satisfy strict scrutiny, which is not met on this record given the law’s broad suppression of disfavored counseling speech.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Colorado’s law can be understood as regulating the professional conduct of licensed mental-health providers in the context of treatment of minors, even though that conduct is carried out through words; under NIFLA, the Court rejected a freestanding “professional speech” doctrine but reaffirmed that States may regulate speech “as part of the practice of” a licensed profession where the regulation sets or enforces standards of care and only incidentally burdens speech. The restriction applies within a fiduciary, state-licensed therapeutic relationship and is justified as a protective measure for minors, aligning with the State’s traditional authority over health and safety regulation and with NIFLA’s recognition of malpractice and informed-consent rules as permissible regulations of professional conduct. On that view, heightened First Amendment scrutiny is not automatically triggered merely because the treatment modality is talk therapy, and Colorado may discipline departures from a legally delineated standard of care without impermissibly targeting public debate or compelled ideological conformity. Given the practical consequences for vulnerable minors and the procedural posture of licensing discipline rather than criminalizing general advocacy, I would uphold the law as applied to professional treatment of minors.
